# Supplementary Information

**Random cell halves are not independent replicates in pooled perturbation screens**

Xuanrui Huang

## Supplementary Table S1 | Non-targeting guides as null perturbations

Each non-targeting guide of the CD4 screen is a separate transduction with no target. Effects are referenced to the mean over the kept non-targeting guides in each half; genes with mean at least 0.1 over non-targeting cells, TCR genes excluded; guides with at least 10 cells per half. Different guides: the first half of one guide against the second half of another, at the same depth, averaged over 50 random pairings (range over pairings in parentheses). Random halves: bootstrap 95% interval over guides. TRBC: variance of the z-score of each guide's TRBC1 fraction (guides with at least 30 cells carrying TRBC counts; in parentheses after permuting guide labels) and the Pearson correlation of the TRBC1 deviation between random halves (at least 15 cells per half).

{TABLE_NTC}

**Cell-line screens.** Raw single cells of the Replogle K562 essential-gene, K562 genome-wide (part 1) and RPE1 screens, the Nadig Jurkat and HepG2 screens and the H1 hESC training data of the 2025 Virtual Cell Challenge; one pseudo-perturbation per non-targeting construct. The last columns compare the mean random-half signal of non-targeting constructs with that of targeting perturbations of the same screen (CD4: resting cells, TCR genes excluded).

{TABLE_NTC_CL}

Non-targeting guides behave like unexpressed targets: almost all look reproducible under random halves, halves from two different guides are positive about half the time, and the cells of each guide come from few clones. Because these guides have no target, guide effects at a target site cannot explain the random-half signal. In the cell-line screens and the H1 data the random-half signal of non-targeting constructs is small, 0.6–7% of that of a typical targeting perturbation, against more than that of a targeting perturbation in CD4.

## Supplementary Table S2 | Same guide against different guides across independent donors

Random halves and guide halves of one donor differ in two ways: guide halves separate the transductions and also the guides. To separate these, we used the released pseudobulk of all four CD4 donors and formed, for each target and state, four pseudobulk effects: guide rank 0 or 1 in donors 1–2 or 3–4 (both sequencing runs pooled; effects relative to the non-targeting controls of the same donors and state; at least 20 cells each). The same four effects were paired in two ways. With the same guide, guide 0 in donors 1–2 was paired with guide 0 in donors 3–4, and likewise for guide 1; with different guides, guide 0 in donors 1–2 was paired with guide 1 in donors 3–4, and vice versa. Both designs separate transductions and donors and differ only in whether the halves share the guide. Values are means over the two pairings of each design; the expressed signal of each pairing is given in parentheses (resting; stimulated). {S5_META}. Cross-half signals are referenced to the null baseline; the context-specific share and the predictor (second implementation) use template-removed responses.

{TABLE_S5}

Guide-specific energy, the same-guide signal minus the different-guide signal, was {S5_RATIO}, relative to the signal shared across guides. It is real: unexpressed targets were also slightly more often positive with the same guide. Transferred to the single-cell data, under the assumption that the across-donor ratio applies within one donor, it accounts for about 8–15% of the random-half signal, against 66–81% that is shared only by cells of one transduction (main text and Methods). The shared-to-specific predictor stayed near zero with the same guide, so its failure across guide halves is not caused by the difference between the guides.

## Supplementary Table S3 | cell-eval 0.8.2 ceilings for all metrics

Resting CD4+ T cells of donor 1: all 300 perturbations, the 150 unexpressed targets and the 150 strength-matched knockdowns, with equal numbers of cells per guide (median 62 per side). Random: the tool's `compute_ceiling` (disjoint random halves of each perturbation and of the controls), range over seeds 0–2. Guide: the tool's `compute` with one guide's cells as "real" and the other's as "prediction", range over the two directions. Values are summarized over the 300 perturbations present in all runs. Asterisks mark metrics whose chance level is 0.5, which the Spearman–Brown correction maps to 0.67. Daggers mark metrics that cell-eval computes over the whole dataset, so they are identical across subsets. Dashes mark metrics that cell-eval did not return for a subset. n.d., not defined: the split-half correlation was at most 0, for which cell-eval returns no ceiling; the half-depth correlation is given in parentheses.

**a, Spearman–Brown corrected ("ceiling").**

**b, Uncorrected half-depth means.**

## Supplementary Table S4 | Structure of unexpressed targets carried by the shared-to-specific predictor

For a pair of contexts X and Y, the predictor maps the shared response of half A, (X_A + Y_A)/2, to the context-specific response of half B, (X_B − Y_B)/2, and gives a held-out prediction F for every perturbation. Because the context-specific response contains +X/2, a predictor that reads the half-A deviation of a perturbation in context X passes that deviation on to F. For a set of targets S, the pass share is 2 Σ_S F · X_B / Σ_S X_A · X_B (with the opposite sign for context Y): the share of the reproducible energy of the targets' own responses in X that reappears in the prediction. Responses were referenced to the mean of the unexpressed targets, and the direction of the mean of all perturbations (the template) was then projected out, so that unexpressed and expressed targets are scored on the same footing. For unexpressed targets, whose knockdown cannot act through the target gene, a pass share comparable to that of expressed targets shows that the predictor carries structure that does not come from the knockdown. The predictor used the top k principal components of the half-A shared response, ridge regression with λ chosen by inner two-fold cross-validation, and two outer folds over perturbations (seed 11). Unexpressed targets are defined per context (in CD4, in both states). CD4 halves are random halves or guide halves; in the cell-line pairs only random halves exist. Intervals are 2.5th–97.5th percentiles over 500 bootstrap resamples of the targets. The shuffled control, which permutes the features across perturbations, gave values of at most {S1_SHUF} in absolute value.

{TABLE_S1}

Under random halves in CD4, the predictor carried the structure of unexpressed targets at the same rate as that of expressed targets; under guide halves it carried neither. In the four cell lines, the pass share of unexpressed targets was 0.6–1.1 times that of expressed targets. In these phenotype-selected libraries the structure of unexpressed targets largely comes from the guides or target sites (Supplementary Fig. S2), so carrying it does not by itself indicate clones.

## Supplementary Table S5 | Robustness of the CD4 results

These analyses used the second implementation of the predictor (two outer and two inner folds; λ chosen by inner cross-validation). Shares of positive unexpressed targets are referenced to the null baseline; the predictor was fitted after template removal.

**CD4.** Targets are either all targets common to the random-half and guide-half designs or the guide-balanced subset, in which the cell numbers of the two guide halves are within a factor of 1.5 of each other in both states (number of targets in parentheses). Genes are all genes kept by the control-mean filter or the 2,000 with the highest control mean. The explained share is given for k = 5, 10, 20 and 50 principal components.

{TABLE_S2_CD4}

Across target sets, gene sets and numbers of components, random halves gave explained shares of 0.13–0.56 in CD4 (0.17–0.51 in donor 1) and guide halves at most 0.002. The guide-balanced subset gave lower random-half values than the full set, and the contrast with guide halves was the same in every row.

## Supplementary Figure S1 | Three-term model: expectations and simulation scenarios

Simulated screens with two contexts, under random halves (red; both halves from one transduction) and independent units (blue; each half from its own transduction), for six scenarios: no unit effect; additive unit states only, with units separate between contexts or shared by them; multiplicative unit gains only, separate or shared; and both terms, shared. **a**, Percentage of null perturbations with a positive cross-half signal; dotted line, 50%. **b**, **c**, Spearman–Brown corrected Pearson ceiling for all perturbations and for null perturbations. **d**, Context-specific share; dashed line, true value. **e**, Explained share of the shared-to-specific predictor; dashed line, true value. **f**, Model and parameters. Additive unit states make null perturbations reproducible and raise both ceilings, under random halves only. Gains leave null perturbations unaffected. The context-specific share changes little in any scenario. Unit effects that are separate between contexts lower the explained share under random halves, and shared gains lower it across independent units. The fabrication and attenuation scenarios are shown in Fig. 5d. Means over three seeds.

## Supplementary Figure S2 | Unexpressed targets in K562 screens

**a**, Share of the within-screen structure of unexpressed targets (n = 178) and expressed targets (n = 651) of the K562 essential-gene library that recurs in an independent K562 screen (genome-wide screen, part 1): summed cross-screen signal divided by the geometric mean of the summed within-screen signals. Error bars, bootstrap 95% intervals over targets (1,000 resamples). Unexpressed targets recur as much as expressed ones, so their structure comes mainly from the guides or target sites, not from clones. **b**, Cross-half signal per target within the day-6 essential-gene screen, within the day-8 genome-wide screen and across the two screens. The non-recurring part of the null signal, (1 − 0.85) × 4.6, is at most about 4% of the expressed signal of 18.4 per target; because it also contains differences between the two screens, it is an upper bound on the clonal part. **c**, K562 genome-wide screen (part 1): share of unexpressed targets with a positive cross-half signal when responses are referenced to the mean of all perturbations (template removed) or to the mean of the unexpressed targets (null baseline), for random halves and for halves formed by sequencing lane. Template removal turns each null perturbation into a reproducible negative template and raises the share. Dashed line, 50%.
